summary: This document specifies the Authentication-Results message header field for email. It records the results of message authentication checks so that mail filters and Mail User Agents can relay the information or use it to sort and filter. It was later replaced by RFC 7601.

plainLanguage.summary: When a mail server checks whether a message really came from the domain it claims, the answer has to travel with the message so that later servers and filters can use it. This RFC defines the header field that carries those answers, in a format that works for every checking scheme.

questions: what does dkim=pass mean in email headers
how do mail servers record spf and dkim results
subtitle: A mail header that records which authentication checks passed, and which did not.

tldr.problem: Several different schemes check whether an email really came from the domain it claims, each with its own result and its own header field, and there was no common place to report them.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication-Results header field names the checking service, then lists one statement per method of the form method=result, with optional supporting data about which message properties were examined.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7001 was obsoleted by RFC 7601 and updated by RFC 7410. The header field reports assertions made upstream rather than proving anything itself, so it is only trustworthy inside a trust boundary, and mail servers must strip incoming copies before adding their own.

facts.label: Methods defined
facts.value: dkim, domainkeys, spf, sender-id, iprev and auth

today: RFC 7001 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 7601, a later revision of the same header field, and it was updated by RFC 7410, which adds a registry for the property types the field uses. It had itself obsoleted RFC 5451 and RFC 6577.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes a header field called Authentication-Results for electronic mail messages that presents the results of a message authentication effort in a machine-readable format. The intent of the header field is to create a place to collect such data when message authentication mechanisms are in use, so that a Mail User Agent and downstream filters can make filtering decisions or provide a recommendation to the user as to the validity of the message's origin and possibly the safety and integrity of its content.

The document revises the original definition found in RFC 5451, based on the various authentication protocols in current use, and incorporates the errata logged since the publication of the original specification.

End users are not expected to be direct consumers of this header field. It is intended for consumption by programs that will use the data or render it in a human-usable form. The document specifies the format and discusses the implications of its presence or absence, but it does not discuss how the data ought to be used, such as what filtering decisions are appropriate or how a user agent might render the results, as those are local policy and user interface design questions.

The published, domain-level email authentication methods in common use at the time of publication are Author Domain Signing Practices, SMTP Service Extension for Authentication, DomainKeys Identified Mail Signatures, Sender Policy Framework, Vouch By Reference, and reverse IP address name validation, which the document calls iprev. Two non-standard methods are recognized but are no longer common: DomainKeys, which is Historic, and Sender ID, which is Experimental.

The specification is not intended to be restricted to domain-based authentication schemes, but the existing schemes in that family have proven a good starting point. The goal is to give current and future schemes a common framework within which to deliver their results to downstream agents and to discourage the creation of unique header fields for each. SPF defined a header field called Received-SPF and the historic DomainKeys defined one called DomainKey-Status, but those carry only their own results and do not meet the requirements. Many SPF implementations have adopted the header field specified here at least as an option, and DomainKeys has been obsoleted by DKIM.

The header field is expected to serve several purposes: conveying the results of various message authentication checks, which are applied by upstream filters and Mail Transfer Agents and then passed to user agents and downstream filters within the same trust domain; providing a common location within a message for this data; and creating an extensible framework for reporting new authentication methods as they emerge. In particular, the mere presence of the header field does not mean its contents are valid: it is reporting assertions made by one or more schemes supposedly applied somewhere upstream. For a consumer to treat those assertions as valid, there must be an assessment of the trust relationship among the consumer, the validating MTA and the mechanism for conveying the information.
sections.plainLanguage: When a mail server checks whether a message really came from the domain it claims, the answer has to travel with the message so that later servers and filters can use it. This RFC defines the header field that carries those answers, in a format that works for every checking scheme.

sections.title: Trust Boundary and Trust Environment
sections.content:
The document makes several references to the trust boundary of an administrative management domain. Given the diversity among existing mail environments, a precise definition is not possible. Simply put, a transfer from the producer of the header field to the consumer must occur within a context that permits the consumer to treat assertions by the producer as being reliable and accurate. How this trust is obtained is outside the scope of the document and is entirely a local matter.

The document therefore defines a trust boundary as the delineation between external and internal entities. Services that are internal, within the trust boundary, are provided by the domain's infrastructure for its users; those that are external are outside its authority. By this definition, hosts within a trust boundary are subject to the domain's authority and policies, independent of their physical placement or operation, so a host inside the boundary might be operated by a remote service provider and reside in that provider's data centre.

A message can be evaluated inside a trust boundary and then depart and re-enter it. An example is a forwarded message carried as a message/rfc822 attachment, or one that is part of a multipart/digest. The details reported by the field cannot be trusted in that case, so the field found within one of those media types is typically ignored.

The content of the header field is meant to convey to consumers that authentication work on the message was already done within its trust boundary, and that those results are being presented. It is not intended to provide message parameters so that consumers can perform authentication protocols on their own.

The header field permits one or more message validation mechanisms to communicate output to one or more separate assessment mechanisms, operating within a unified trust boundary. The field often contains no integrity or validation mechanism of its own, so its presence must be trusted implicitly. Valid use of the header field therefore requires removing any occurrences of it that are present when the message enters the domain, so that later occurrences have been added within the trust boundary.

The document also separates two words that are often confused. Authorization is the establishment of permission to use a resource or represent an identity; in this context it indicates that a message from a particular domain arrived via a route the domain has explicitly approved. Authentication is the assertion of validity of a piece of data about a message, such as the sender's identity, or of the message in its entirety. SPF and Sender ID are authorization mechanisms, because they express a result that shows whether the domain that apparently sent the message has explicitly authorized the connecting SMTP client to relay messages on its behalf, but they do not validate any other property of the message. DKIM, by contrast, is agnostic as to the routing of a message but uses cryptographic signatures to authenticate agents, assign some responsibility for the message, which implies authorization, and ensure that the listed portions of the message were not modified in transit. Because the signatures are not tied to SMTP connections, they can be added by the domain of origin, intermediate domains such as a mailing list server, other handling agents, or any combination. Rather than create a separate header field for each class of solution, the proposal groups them both into a single header field.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is only worth reading if you trust the server that wrote it. Inside one organisation's mail system the servers can vouch for each other; across the internet they cannot. So the field is only meaningful for mail that stayed inside the organisation that checked it, and anything arriving from outside has to have its copy removed.

sections.title: The Header Field Format
sections.content:
The header field is called Authentication-Results. It is a Structured Header Field as defined in the Internet Message Format specification, so all of the related definitions there apply. It is added at the top of the message as it transits the mail servers that do authentication checks, so some idea of how far away the checks were done can be inferred. It is therefore considered a trace field, and the related definitions there apply as well.

The value of the header field, after removing comments, consists of an authentication identifier, an optional version, and then a series of statements and supporting data. The statements are of the form method=result and indicate which authentication methods were applied and their respective results. For each statement the supporting data can include a reason string and one or more property=value statements indicating which message properties were evaluated to reach that conclusion. The header field can appear more than once in a single message, more than one result can be represented in a single header field, or a combination of these can be applied.

Formally, the header field is specified in Augmented Backus-Naur Form as authres-header = "Authentication-Results:" [CFWS] authserv-id [ CFWS authres-version ] ( no-result / 1*resinfo ) [CFWS] CRLF. The authserv-id is a value identifying the authentication service. The authres-version is one or more digits indicating which version of this specification is in use; this specification is version 1, and the absence of a version implies this version. The special case none is used to indicate that no message authentication was performed. A resinfo is a semicolon followed by a method specification and optionally a reason specification and any number of property specifications. A method specification is a method name, optionally with a version, an equals sign, and a result. A property specification has the form ptype.property = pvalue.

The ptype is one of four values. smtp indicates that the property was a parameter to an SMTP command, header that it was a value taken from a message header field, body that it was some property of the message body, and policy that it was some other property evaluated by the receiving server. The special SMTP verbs mailfrom and rcptto cover the two-word commands, and a server reporting one of them converts the command to lowercase and drops the spaces, so MAIL FROM becomes mailfrom.

The policy ptype indicates that some local policy mechanism was applied that augments or even replaces the result returned by the authentication mechanism. The property and value identify the local policy that was applied and the result it returned. The document's example is that a DKIM signature is not required to include the Subject header field among the signed fields, so a domain receiving such a message might decide that such a signature is unacceptable even though it passes, because the Subject could be altered after signing. Such a domain could replace the DKIM pass result with a policy result and add policy.dkim-rules=unsigned-subject. The property names are arbitrary, chosen by the domain using them, and are not normally registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The header starts with the name of the service that did the checking, then a list of statements like dkim=pass or spf=fail. Each statement can carry a reason and a note about which part of the message was examined, such as the sender's address or a particular header field.

sections.title: Methods and Result Values
sections.content:
Each individual authentication method returns one of a set of specific result values. Verifiers SHOULD use these values as described, and new methods not specified in the document MUST include a similar result table either in their defining documents or in supplementary ones.

DKIM is represented by the dkim method and DomainKeys by the domainkeys method. A signature is acceptable to the domain if it passes local policy checks, or there are no specific local policy checks. Both use the same result set. none means the message was not signed. pass means it was signed, the signatures were acceptable, and they passed verification. fail means it was signed and the signatures were acceptable but failed verification. policy means it was signed but some aspect of the signature was not acceptable. neutral means it was signed but the signatures contained syntax errors or could not otherwise be processed, and is also used for other failures not covered elsewhere. temperror means the message could not be verified due to an error likely to be transient, such as a temporary inability to retrieve a public key, and a later attempt may produce a final result. permerror means it could not be verified due to an unrecoverable error, such as a required header field being absent, and a later attempt is unlikely to produce a final result. DKIM advises that a message failing verification is to be treated as unsigned; a report of fail permits the receiver to decide how to handle the failure, while a report of neutral or none preempts that choice.

SPF and Sender ID use the spf and sender-id method names. The SPF result values are none, pass, fail, softfail, policy, neutral, temperror and permerror. An additional result of policy is defined for both, meaning the client was authorized to inject or relay mail on behalf of the sender's DNS domain according to the method's algorithm, but local policy dictates that the result is unacceptable. For example, policy might be used if SPF returns a pass but a local policy check matches the sending domain to an explicit list of unacceptable domains.

The iprev method, defined in a later section, uses pass, fail, temperror and permerror, and has no none, because any TCP connection delivering email has an IP address associated with it, so some kind of evaluation will always be possible. SMTP AUTH is represented by the auth method with none, pass, fail, temperror and permerror. Result codes were also registered in other documents for Vouch By Reference, represented by vbr, Authorized Third-Party Signatures, represented by dkim-atps, and Author Domain Signing Practices, represented by dkim-adsp.

Extension methods and extension result codes may be defined in future revisions or extensions. They are registered with IANA and preferably published in an RFC. Extension methods can be defined to allow additional information from new authentication systems to be communicated, or to allow sub-identifiers that indicate different levels of authentication, such as auth1-weak and auth1-strong. Experimental method identifiers must only be used within domains that have explicitly consented to use them, and are subject to change at any time, so any server intended for production use SHOULD ignore or delete a header field that includes an experimental method identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Every method reports the same small set of outcomes: it passed, it failed, there was nothing to check, there was a temporary problem, there was a permanent problem, or local policy overrode the answer. The names differ slightly between methods, so a reader has to know which method produced which result.

sections.title: Adding and Removing the Header Field
sections.content:
The specification makes no attempt to evaluate the relative strengths of the various methods. The methods listed are an order-independent set; their sequence does not indicate relative strength or importance of one over another. It is for the consumer to interpret the result of each method based on its own knowledge of what that method evaluates.

An MTA compliant with this specification adds the header field, after performing one or more message authentication tests, to indicate which server or domain performed the test, which test was applied and what the result was. If it applies more than one test, it adds the header field either once per test or once indicating all of the results. An MTA MUST NOT add a result to an existing header field. It MAY add a header field containing only the authentication identifier and the none token, to indicate explicitly that no message authentication schemes were applied before delivery.

Adding header fields in order, at the top, is particularly important, and this header field SHOULD be inserted above any other trace header fields that servers prepend. This placement allows easy detection of header fields that can be trusted. An MTA adding the header field has to take steps to identify it as legitimate to the consumers that will ultimately read it, and the document does not mandate any specific solution, since each environment has its own facilities and limitations.

Most known authentication methods focus on a particular identifier to evaluate. SPF and Sender ID differ in that they can yield a result based on more than one identifier: SPF can evaluate the HELO parameter or the MailFrom parameter, and Sender ID can evaluate the MailFrom parameter or the Purported Responsible Address identity. When reporting those results, only the parameter that yielded the result is included. An MTA adding the header field SHOULD NOT include any data that has not been authenticated by the methods being applied, and user agents SHOULD NOT render such information to users if it is presented by a method known not to authenticate it.

Consumers SHOULD NOT interpret the header field unless specifically configured to do so by the user or administrator, and SHOULD NOT interpret it unless the authentication service identifier it bears appears to be one used within its own domain as configured by the user or administrator. They MUST ignore any result reported using a result value not in the IANA Result Code registry, or a ptype not listed in the corresponding registry, and MUST ignore a result indicated for any method they do not specifically support.

For security reasons, any MTA conforming to this specification MUST delete any discovered instance of this header field that claims, by virtue of its authentication service identifier, to have been added within its trust boundary but that did not come directly from another trusted MTA. For simplicity and maximum security, a border MTA could remove all instances on mail crossing into its trust boundary, but this may conflict with the desire to access results performed by trusted external providers, and may invalidate signed messages whose signatures cover those instances. A more robust border MTA could allow a specific list of authenticating servers whose information is admitted, removing the header field originating from all others. An MTA SHOULD remove any instance bearing a version it does not support, but MUST remove such a header field if the SMTP connection relaying the message is not from a trusted internal MTA.
sections.plainLanguage: The checking server adds the header at the very top of the message, so that its position shows how far the message has travelled since the check. Every server inside the organisation has to remove any copy that arrived from outside, otherwise a stranger could claim the message was checked when it was not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
On forged header fields, a user agent or filter that accesses a mailbox whose messages are handled by a non-conformant MTA could make false conclusions based on forged header fields. A malicious user or agent could forge a header field using the DNS domain of a receiving domain as the identifier and claim that the message was properly authenticated. The non-conformant MTA would fail to strip the forged field, and the user agent could inappropriately trust it. For this reason, it is best not to have processing of the header field enabled by default; instead it should be ignored, at least for the purposes of enacting filtering decisions, unless specifically enabled by the user or administrator after verifying that the border MTA is compliant. It is acceptable for a user agent to have an explicit list of hostnames whose header fields are trustworthy, but this list should initially be empty.

Several alternative mechanisms are listed as having been proposed but not developed due to lack of demand: a digital signature protecting the header field that the user agent could verify with a posted public key; a way to interrogate the MTA that added the field to confirm it actually provides authentication services and saw the message; a way to interrogate the internal servers that apparently handled the message, based on Received header fields; extensions to IMAP, SMTP and POP3 that would let a user agent acquire the identifier in use within a domain; and using the position of the field, which should always appear above a Received header added by a trusted server, as a test for validity. Mitigation can also be accomplished by moving the results into message metadata carried by an SMTP extension, so that there is no vector for forgery by an outside agent.

On misleading results, until some form of service for querying the reputation of a sending agent is widely deployed, the existence of a pass result does not render a message trustworthy. It is possible for spam to pass several of the methods, for example a piece of spam signed using DKIM by the originator of the spam, which might be a spammer or a compromised system. This issue is not resolved by removing forged header fields, so user agents and filters must take some care even after malicious headers are scrubbed.

On denial of service, a verifier wishing to report the iprev result needs to take care not to go to unbounded lengths to resolve A and PTR queries, because a DNS-based denial-of-service attack exists for verifiers that attempt DNS-based identity verification of arriving connections. A user agent making use of an iprev result needs to be aware of the algorithm the reporting verifier used and especially its limitations.

Failing to follow the instruction to reject at the border rather than add a header field can result in a denial-of-service attack caused by the generation of delivery status notifications to addresses that did not send the rejected messages, which is colloquially known as backscatter. A compliant installation will also have to include, at each server, a list of other servers known to be compliant and trustworthy, and failing to keep that list current as the internal infrastructure changes may expose the domain to attack. Finally, if an attack becomes known against an authentication method, an agent verifying that method can be fooled into thinking an inauthentic message is authentic, and the value of the header field becomes misleading.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things can go wrong. A forged header can make a message look checked when it was not, and a genuine pass result does not mean the message is good, because a spammer can sign its own spam perfectly. So the header is evidence about the domain, not about the message.

data.title: Authentication-Results
data.code:
authres-header = "Authentication-Results:" [CFWS] authserv-id
              [ CFWS authres-version ]
              ( no-result / 1*resinfo ) [CFWS] CRLF

no-result = [CFWS] ";" [CFWS] "none"

resinfo = [CFWS] ";" methodspec [ CFWS reasonspec ]
              *( CFWS propspec )

methodspec = [CFWS] method [CFWS] "=" [CFWS] result

propspec = ptype [CFWS] "." [CFWS] property [CFWS] "=" pvalue

ptype = "smtp" / "header" / "body" / "policy"

viz.caption: THE DKIM AND DOMAINKEYS RESULT VALUES

items.label: Accepted and verified
items.desc: The message was signed, the signatures were acceptable, and they passed verification.

items.label: Accepted but failed
items.desc: The message was signed and the signatures were acceptable, but they failed verification.

items.label: Rejected by policy
items.desc: The message was signed, but some aspect of the signature was not acceptable.

items.label: Could not be processed
items.desc: The signatures contained syntax errors or could not otherwise be processed.

items.label: Temporary problem
items.desc: The message could not be verified because of an error likely to be transient, such as a temporary inability to retrieve a public key.

items.label: Permanent problem
items.desc: The message could not be verified because of an unrecoverable error, such as a required header field being absent.

viz.caption: THE PIECES OF THE MAIL PATH THAT MATTER HERE

items.title: Border MTA
items.text: The server that sits between the internet and the organisation's users. It usually does the authentication checks.

items.title: Intermediate MTA
items.text: Any server that is neither a delivery server nor the first one to handle the message.

items.title: Delivery MTA
items.text: The server that actually puts the message into a user's mailbox.

items.title: Producer and consumer
items.text: The producer adds the header; the consumer reads it and decides what to do about it.
